The Fed’s March 15, 2020 actions acknowledge a sharp, negative near-term demand shock from COVID-19, but they also deploy tools that the literature suggests can materially blunt financial amplification and support recovery. By cutting the policy rate to the effective lower bound and launching large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, the Fed eases broad financial conditions and stabilizes key markets—consistent with the liquidity effect and open-market-operations mechanisms emphasized in monetary theory (e.g., Eichenbaum–Fuerst; Stockman; New York Fed operating procedures). Reinforced discount-window terms, ample repo operations, and coordinated dollar swap lines address dollar funding strains and sustain the flow of credit, aligning with the credit/bank-lending channel evidence that alleviating external finance premia limits downturns (Bernanke–Gertler credit view; Oliner and Rudebusch; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein; Gertler and Gilchrist). With market-based inflation compensation falling and survey-based long-run expectations little changed, the stance is also consistent with inflation-forecast-targeting guidance (Svensson) and the view that, when inflation is below target and a liquidity-trap risk looms, balance-sheet policies and strong forward guidance are appropriate. Netting these considerations, the near-term outlook remains negative due to the pandemic shock, but decisive policy lowers tail risks and improves medium-term prospects relative to an unmitigated scenario.
